properties.title: My Home
properties.desc_l:
In 2014, my father built our home in Bandutia, near the Kaliganga River, and I moved here. I have lived here since then.

The Kaliganga is the river with which I am most connected. I have spent a great deal of time around it, and it is deeply embedded in the life of Manikganj. The town itself developed around the river, and many everyday social and cultural activities still gather around it—from places for adda to restaurants and other meeting places.

Eventually, the river became more than a familiar landscape. My undergraduate dissertation examined changes in its morphology and how people perceive and experience those changes. I returned to the river as a researcher, trying to understand not only how a river changes physically, but how those changes become part of people's understanding of their own place.

properties.title: Early Childhood
properties.desc_l: My early childhood was spent largely around Uttar Seuta. This was where my first friendships were formed and where much of my early outlook towards the world developed. Before I had any language for geography, this neighbourhood was already teaching me something about place: how people live together, how relationships form around particular spaces, and how a familiar locality becomes part of one's sense of the world.

properties.title: The Pendulous Teenage
properties.desc_l:
My teenage years unfolded in a quieter place near my school, where I could see a regional highway from my study desk. The highway became an accidental observatory.

I began noticing that movement was never random. In the morning, school students moved along the road; then came office workers and people travelling for other purposes. Later, when the school bell rang, the movement changed again, followed by children heading out to play. The road appeared to me as an artery connecting people to different spaces of interaction, with movement bound to particular times of the day.

I did not know it then, but I was beginning to look at the world spatially.

properties.title: Primary Education
properties.desc_l: My formal education began at the Experimental School attached to the Primary Teachers' Training Institute in Manikganj. The school was also a kind of laboratory for trainee teachers learning how to teach. Its large campus gave us plenty of room to explore, play and grow. Looking back, education here was not only what happened inside the classroom; the campus itself was part of the experience of learning.

properties.title: Secondary Education
properties.desc_l:
Secondary school was where curiosity began turning into projects. With friends, I made plans, formed teams and pursued ideas ranging from investigating supposedly haunted places to creating imaginary political parties. It was a mixture of curiosity, storytelling and organization, and many of the things I still write and think about have their roots in this period—only in a more mature form now.

The school pond and its ghat were among my favourite places. I spent long periods there thinking about the future and developing story plots. Around the same time, I began writing my first blog, experimenting with HTML and writing my first stories. The world of newspapers and their emphasis on science also contributed to this growing curiosity.

properties.title: Hiigher Secondary Education
properties.desc_l:
Higher secondary education brought me into a district-level college where we were among the youngest students. Academically, this period did not leave as strong an impression on me as some of the stages before or after it. But being surrounded by more mature people and seeing the consequences of how people navigate life gave me a different kind of education.

It was less about textbooks and more about learning how society works, sometimes by watching what happens when people move through it recklessly.

properties.title: Undergraduate Life
properties.desc_l:
After a long admission season involving more than a hundred admission tests, I eventually found myself in an unexpected place: the Department of Geography and Environment at Jahangirnagar University.



I had initially imagined studying subjects such as CSE or ETE, partly because science and engineering are so strongly promoted in Bangladesh. But I was never entirely an engineering-minded person. What I had always been interested in was the complexity of human minds and societies. I simply did not know that geography existed as a discipline capable of bringing many of those questions together.



At Jahangirnagar, geography became a tool for asking questions I had been carrying for years. The world began revealing itself in greater detail: through landscapes, societies, fieldwork, maps and spatial relationships.



Field trips were equally important. They taught me that analysing geography requires encountering places directly—observing landscapes, people and processes before attempting to represent them through data.



Several teachers shaped this way of thinking in different directions: Dr. Nurul Islam helped me understand complex river morphology and hydraulics; Dr. Shamsul Alam taught me to look carefully at the physical Earth through geomorphology; and Dr. Nayeem Aziz Ansari expanded my engagement with human geography, including its capacity for critique and satire.



The university also gave me people from different backgrounds and places, and among those relationships I met the person who would become my wife and who now shares the rest of this journey with me.

properties.title: Journey with IRSGIS, JU
properties.desc_l:
My introduction to GIS, remote sensing and research developed through the Institute of Remote Sensing and GIS at Jahangirnagar University, under my mentor Dr. Sheikh Tawhidul Islam.

But what I learned here was not simply how to operate GIS software. I began to understand spatial science as a way of answering questions. One of the most important lessons was learning how quantitative methods can be used to investigate questions that are fundamentally qualitative.

This was where geography became more than a subject for me. It became a way of thinking.

properties.title: Journey with ICCCAD, IUB
properties.desc_l:
My involvement with the International Centre for Climate Change and Development began unexpectedly, when I became a trainee in its youth development programme.

I had already experienced disasters firsthand in Manikganj, and those experiences had drawn me towards environmental and climate questions. At ICCCAD, that interest developed through conferences, programmes and eventually an internship involving Nature-based Solutions, Climate Services and Climate Finance.

The experience introduced me to climate change not simply as an environmental phenomenon, but as a field involving science, policy, institutions and activism. Here, science often came first: understanding the evidence and translating that knowledge into action.

properties.title: Journey with Waterkeepers Consortium, Bangladesh
properties.desc_l:
My second major internship took me closer to the ground level of environmental problems through Waterkeepers Bangladesh.

Here, I worked around water pollution and saw a different relationship between knowledge and action. If ICCCAD had shown me how science can inform high-level climate work and activism, Waterkeepers showed me how activism can begin with people and their everyday environmental realities—and how scientific understanding can be validated and made meaningful through that engagement.

The contrast between the two experiences became important to how I understood environmental problems: science and people cannot really be separated.

properties.title: Post Graduate Study
properties.desc_l:
After studying geography and working around climate and environmental issues, I wanted to understand climate change more deeply as a science.

I therefore began my master's at the Institute of Water and Flood Management at BUET. I also carried a particular idea with me: climate science often makes powerful use of physical models and climate data, but the spatial dimension of those problems can be much more deeply explored through GIS and geographic thinking.

My thesis brought these interests together by examining the involvement of spatial predictors in physics-based climate modelling, using GIS and deep learning for climate-model data downscaling.

For me, this was not a departure from geography. It was an attempt to carry geographical thinking into climate science.

properties.title: Journey with Esri Bangladesh
properties.desc_l:
My formal professional life began at Esri Bangladesh.

Starting work here gave me something of a shock. The GIS I had known at university was only a small part of what GIS could actually be. Professional practice showed me that GIS is not fundamentally about producing maps.

A map can be an output, but GIS can be much more than that. It can become the connective fabric between an institution's data, its processes, its decisions and the work carried out around those decisions.

This changed the way I understand my own profession. I no longer see GIS simply as a technical method for representing geography. I see it as infrastructure for connecting spatial knowledge with action.

properties.title: Hello World!
properties.desc_l: I was born here, at Dhaka Medical College Hospital, on 12 September 1997. This is where the mapped journey begins—not yet with a particular direction, but with a life that would gradually become increasingly concerned with places, people, movement and the ways they shape one another.

properties.title: Maternal Home
properties.desc_l: My maternal home lies in the floodplain of the Dhaleshwari River. During the monsoon, water surrounds the houses and the familiar landscape turns into a collection of islands. In winter, the same landscape changes again, often becoming yellow with mustard fields. Much of my earliest experience of rural Bangladesh came from here: learning to walk, learning to read, communicating with people and becoming familiar with a landscape that never remained quite the same throughout the year.

properties.title: Paternal Home
properties.desc_l: My paternal home is only a few kilometres from my maternal home, within the same broader landscape and culture. Rather than being a completely different world, it became another part of the same rural geography in which I grew up. Spending time here introduced me to the rhythms of rural life and to the people whose everyday lives, problems and relationships with their surroundings would eventually become questions I would try to understand through geography.

properties.title: In Laws
properties.desc_l:
Marriage introduced another geography into my life.

My in-laws' home is in a Himalayan piedmont district, a landscape quite different from the floodplain environment in which I grew up. The contrast is not simply physical. The two places carry different landscapes, cultures and ways of inhabiting space.

Moving between these places has given me another opportunity to experience how geography becomes part of everyday life—not as an abstract division on a map, but through differences in landscape, culture and the ways people relate to where they live.
